body:
Fireflies.ai Meeting Transcript

Title: POC scoping - Aurora CX Customer Support AI (success criteria, evals, access)
Date: Dec 2, 2025
Time: 10:03 AM - 10:50 AM PST
Duration: 47 min

Attendees:
- Priyom Das (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Sales Engineering)
- Simran Kaur (Redwood Inference, Enterprise Demo Architect)
- Jamie Chen (Aurora CX, Director Support Ops)
- Rohan Mehta (Aurora CX, Staff ML Engineer)
- Elena Garcia (Aurora CX, Support Platform PM)
- Dinesh Patel (Aurora CX, Security/IT)

Auto-summary (generated):
Aurora CX and Redwood aligned on a 2–3 week POC for a customer support AI workflow (ticket summarization + suggested response) with emphasis on predictable latency/cost at scale. The group defined measurable success criteria (quality thresholds via rubric + acceptance rate, p95 latency targets, and unit cost guardrails), discussed evaluation design (prompt set, structured outputs, regression checks), and clarified access needs for a dedicated demo/POC project with least-privilege API keys and synthetic-only data. Redwood will provision isolated demo-tenant resources and share a written plan; Aurora will provide synthetic sample tickets and target outputs.

Topics:
- POC scope and timeline
- Workflows: summarization, intent/routing, response drafting
- Throughput + latency targets
- Evaluation prompts, rubrics, and regression gating
- Model pinning, fallbacks, and reliability story
- Demo tenant / POC project access + key scoping
- Security notes: logs, retention, and synthetic data

Action items:
- Priyom (Redwood): Send recap + proposed POC success criteria + timeline by 2025-12-02
- Markus (Redwood): Provision Aurora POC project + scoped key in demo tenant by 2025-12-03
- Simran (Redwood): Share throughput sizing assumptions + suggested batching/caching toggles by 2025-12-04
- Jamie/Rohan (Aurora): Provide synthetic ticket set + desired outputs/rubric notes by 2025-12-05
- Dinesh (Aurora): Confirm any IP allowlist / SSO requirement for the POC project by 2025-12-05

Questions (captured):
- Can we guarantee the model doesn’t change mid-POC?
- What happens if capacity is constrained during a live test?
- How do we see token-level cost + latency breakdown by route?
- Can responses be forced into JSON for our downstream tooling?
- What does “Dedicated” look like later if POC succeeds?

Transcript:

[00:00] Priyom Das: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is pretty simple: scope what “good” looks like for the POC, agree on the exact workflow we’re testing, and then make sure we can get you access without the usual demo-tenant, like, weirdness. Markus and Simran are here for the technical bits.

[00:18] Jamie Chen: Sounds good. We wanna keep this tight, like two to three weeks, and we need to be able to tell leadership, “yes, this will reduce handle time,” or “no.”

[00:30] Rohan Mehta: And from my side, I need to know if the serving layer is gonna be stable. We’ve been burned by, you know, model changes and rate limit surprises.

[00:43] Markus Klein: Totally. That’s actually why we’ve been building this repeatable demo tenant thing. For a POC we’ll pin model versions and we can set explicit quota so you’re not discovering 429s during testing.

[01:03] Elena Garcia: Quick context: Our use case is Zendesk-like, but internal. Agents see a ticket, we want a short summary, suggested next action, and optionally a drafted response. We also route to a macro library.

[01:18] Priyom Das: Great. So, two workflows or three? (1) Summarize ticket + classify, (2) draft response with citations or constraints, (3) maybe rerank macros. What’s the must-have?

[01:34] Jamie Chen: Must-have is summary + suggested response. Classification is nice, but if we have to pick, it’s those two.

[01:46] Rohan Mehta: We also care about format. We need structured output because it goes into our agent UI. If we get a big blob of text we spend a week parsing.

[01:56] Simran Kaur: Yep. We can do structured outputs. We usually demo it as JSON schema. Not perfect every time, but we can set up a constrained format and do retries if it fails validation.

[02:12] Rohan Mehta: When you say “retries,” is that like client side or server side?

[02:16] Simran Kaur: Either. Our SDK examples do client-side with idempotency keys. On the platform we also have policies like “if invalid JSON, run one corrective pass.” We can show both.

[02:30] Priyom Das: Let’s define success criteria in three buckets: quality, performance, and economics. Jamie, how do you want to judge quality?

[02:39] Jamie Chen: Agent acceptance rate. Like if the drafted response is usable with minimal edits. We can do a rubric: accurate, tone, policy compliant, doesn’t promise refunds, that kind of thing.

[02:55] Elena Garcia: Also “no hallucinated policies.” That’s been a big problem.

[03:00] Markus Klein: Got it. So we’ll need an eval set. Ideally 25 to 50 synthetic tickets, and then you provide what “good” looks like. Even if it’s bullet points.

[03:13] Rohan Mehta: We can generate synthetic. We cannot use real customer tickets. Just to be clear.

[03:18] Markus Klein: Same. Demo tenant is synthetic-only. And for logging, we can disable payload logging and only keep metrics. We’ll keep that in mind.

[03:28] Dinesh Patel: Yeah I’m gonna ask about logs. If prompts are stored, that’s a no.

[03:34] Simran Kaur: Understood. For the demo/POC project, we can set retention to minimal and not store request bodies. You still get token counts and latency, but not the content.

[03:47] Dinesh Patel: Okay. Also do you support SSO for access?

[03:51] Priyom Das: For the production product yes, SSO/SAML and RBAC. For the demo tenant we typically do user invites + roles. But we can keep it just API key access for the POC if that’s easier.

[04:04] Dinesh Patel: API key is fine as long as it’s scoped.

[04:08] Markus Klein: Yeah, least-privilege. We can scope to a single project, specific endpoints, and we can rotate it weekly.

[04:20] Priyom Das: On performance: what’s your throughput target? Like how many tickets per minute do you need to process, or is it real-time per agent?

[04:29] Jamie Chen: For agents, it needs to feel instant-ish. If they click “draft response,” they won’t wait 15 seconds. For offline, we do backlog sweeps too.

[04:40] Rohan Mehta: Let’s quantify. For interactive: p95 under 2.5 seconds for summary, maybe under 4 seconds for draft. For batch: we might do 20k tickets overnight.

[04:54] Simran Kaur: Helpful. When you say 2.5 seconds, is that end-to-end including network?

[04:59] Rohan Mehta: End-to-end from our service in us-west. Assume 200ms network.

[05:05] Simran Kaur: Okay. We can set a route in the demo tenant pinned to a specific model variant. We’ll measure time-to-first-token and full completion.

[05:16] Markus Klein: And we can use streaming for the draft response. Agents perceive it as faster. You’ll get tokens as they come.

[05:24] Jamie Chen: Streaming is good. But our UI wants the JSON at the end.

[05:28] Markus Klein: That’s fine. Stream for the “draft_text” field and then finalize with valid JSON. (Sometimes people do “text stream” and then parse at end.)

[05:39] Rohan Mehta: Cost-wise, leadership is very sensitive. We need to see per-ticket cost.

[05:45] Priyom Das: Totally. In Console you’ll see token-level breakdown: prompt tokens, output tokens, latency, and the dollar-ish unit costs. And you can compare toggles like caching/batching.

[05:59] Elena Garcia: What toggles do you mean?

[06:01] Simran Kaur: Like continuous batching. Or prefix caching if you have a stable system prompt and policy text. It reduces cost, sometimes improves throughput, but it can impact latency depending on settings.

[06:16] Rohan Mehta: Do we control that, or you control it?

[06:19] Simran Kaur: You can control at the route level. For demo/POC, we can set two routes: “low-latency” and “low-cost.” Then you can run the same eval set against both.

[06:32] Priyom Das: That becomes a nice story: you pick the SLO, we make the serving behavior predictable.

[06:40] Jamie Chen: Okay but don’t overcomplicate it. We need one path that’s acceptable.

[06:46] Priyom Das: Yep, we’ll keep it simple. For success criteria: maybe (a) 70% agent accept with minimal edits on synthetic set, (b) p95 latency under X, (c) cost per ticket under Y. Do you have a target for Y?

[07:02] Jamie Chen: We have a budget number, but I don’t want to say it on the call. Rohan can share offline.

[07:09] Rohan Mehta: I can send a range. It’s not crazy low, but we need to show it’s not gonna balloon.

[07:16] Markus Klein: We can also show the breakdown so you can see why it’s ballooning: long prompts, too-long outputs, etc.

[07:24] Priyom Das: On model stability: you mentioned you’ve been burned. For the POC we’ll pin model version. If we do a fallback, it’s controlled and only if the primary is unavailable.

[07:36] Rohan Mehta: Define “fallback.” Like a different model? That can ruin evals.

[07:41] Simran Kaur: Right. For POC we can actually disable fallback during eval runs. For interactive you might want it on, because if a region hiccups you’d rather get an answer than error. But we can tag those events.

[07:56] Rohan Mehta: That’s good. I want a clean eval mode.

[08:00] Markus Klein: We also have a healthcheck endpoint in the demo environment that checks quota, model availability, and dashboard ingestion. SEs use it before demos; we can run it before your load tests.

[08:14] Elena Garcia: How do we generate load without writing a ton of harness code?

[08:18] Markus Klein: We have a small scenario runner in our examples repo. It can replay a dataset of prompts, do concurrency, and export results. Not perfect, but it’s quick.

[08:30] Rohan Mehta: If it exports JSONL with latencies, that’s enough.

[08:33] Simran Kaur: Yep, and we can also pipe it into your Grafana if you want, but that’s probably extra.

[08:41] Priyom Das: Let’s talk timeline. If we provision access tomorrow, you can start with your synthetic tickets by end of week, then we run eval early next week, then load test.

[08:54] Jamie Chen: That’s fine. We need a midpoint check-in though.

[08:58] Priyom Das: We’ll do a 30-min checkpoint next Thursday.

[09:04] Dinesh Patel: One more on security: where is this running? Like region.

[09:08] Markus Klein: Demo tenant is in US regions. For production, we support more and can do VPC/private deployments. For POC we keep it hosted, but we can walk you through the Private architecture.

[09:22] Dinesh Patel: Okay, so no PHI, no regulated data. Synthetic only. Good.

[09:29] Jamie Chen: For eval prompts, what do you need from us?

[09:32] Simran Kaur: Ideally: the ticket text, the desired summary style (like 3 bullets), and response constraints. Example: “don’t mention refunds,” “ask for order ID,” “be friendly but concise.” If you have policy snippets, we can include them as context.

[09:49] Elena Garcia: We do have a policy doc but it’s internal.

[09:52] Jamie Chen: We can redact and summarize it.

[09:55] Markus Klein: Great. Also we should decide the structured schema. Like:
- summary_bullets: string array
- customer_sentiment: enum
- recommended_next_action: enum
- draft_response: string
- confidence: number

[10:12] Rohan Mehta: Confidence is always fake though.

[10:14] Markus Klein: (laughs) Fair. Optional. We can do “needs_human_review: boolean” instead.

[10:21] Jamie Chen: That’s actually useful.

[10:24] Priyom Das: Can we align on the evaluation metric? Like: “pass” if summary is accurate and response is policy compliant.

[10:32] Rohan Mehta: We do pairwise comparisons too. Like compare Model A vs Model B.

[10:37] Simran Kaur: We can support that. In the demo tenant we can set two routes pinned to two models, then run the same prompt set and do side-by-side.

[10:49] Priyom Das: For procurement, you’ll want a clean story: why Redwood vs just calling OpenAI/Anthropic directly. The main thing we’ll show is serving controls: predictability, routing, observability, unit economics.

[11:03] Jamie Chen: That’s the pitch we need internally, yeah.

[11:07] Rohan Mehta: But if the quality isn’t there, none of that matters.

[11:10] Priyom Das: Agreed. That’s why we’re grounding this in your eval set.

[11:16] (cross talk)

[11:18] Elena Garcia: Sorry, can I ask: are we using your native endpoint or OpenAI-compatible?

[11:23] Markus Klein: For POC, whichever is easier. If you already have OpenAI client code, we can do OpenAI-compat. Native SDK gives you better access to route configs and telemetry.

[11:36] Rohan Mehta: We can start with OpenAI-compat. Less code.

[11:39] Simran Kaur: Cool. We’ll still configure routes on our side.

[11:44] Priyom Das: Access details: we’ll create a separate project inside the demo tenant so you’re not sharing with other demos. You’ll get one API key with scopes, and we’ll set a quota that matches your planned tests.

[11:59] Rohan Mehta: What quota are we talking?

[12:01] Simran Kaur: We can start with, say, 2 million tokens/day for the first week, then adjust. For load testing we might spike; we can do a temporary increase.

[12:13] Rohan Mehta: Okay. And rate limit? We might run 50 concurrent.

[12:17] Markus Klein: We can set per-minute request limits high enough, or you can coordinate. Also batching changes the effective throughput.

[12:26] Jamie Chen: We need to avoid “oops 429” during the executive review.

[12:30] Markus Klein: Understood. We’ll set headroom and we’ll have a healthcheck you can run before the exec session.

[12:38] Priyom Das: Switching gears: what’s the “demo moment” you want at the end? Like show one ticket live, show the console graphs, show cost per ticket.

[12:48] Jamie Chen: Ideally: show a bad ticket and how it produces a safe response. Then show numbers: latency and cost.

[12:55] Elena Garcia: And show we can roll out safely. Like a canary.

[12:59] Simran Kaur: We can do a small canary demo: route version A vs version B, 10% traffic, and show rollback. For POC we can keep it synthetic traffic.

[13:14] Rohan Mehta: I’m interested in the tracing too. Like where time is spent.

[13:18] Markus Klein: We have per-request traces and error analysis. If JSON validation fails, you’ll see it.

[13:28] Dinesh Patel: Just make sure traces don’t include payload.

[13:31] Markus Klein: Yep, we’ll configure it.

[13:35] Priyom Das: Okay, let’s lock success criteria draft:
1) Quality: on a 30-ticket synthetic set, at least 80% of outputs pass rubric for “accurate summary” and “policy compliant draft,” and at least 60% “agent ready with minimal edits.”
2) Performance: interactive route p95 < 4.0s for draft, p95 < 2.5s for summary, measured from Aurora service in us-west.
3) Economics: target cost per ticket within the range you’ll share offline; Redwood to provide token breakdown and levers to reduce.

[14:11] Jamie Chen: That’s close. The 80/60 split seems okay. We’ll confirm after we see examples.

[14:18] Rohan Mehta: Also add: no more than 2% invalid JSON outputs. If schema breaks, it breaks our UI.

[14:25] Simran Kaur: Great call. We can implement retry-on-invalid and measure the raw failure rate vs corrected.

[14:33] Priyom Das: Perfect. Next: what do you need from us today? Anything blocking?

[14:38] Rohan Mehta: We need the endpoint, key, and a sample prompt template.

[14:42] Markus Klein: We’ll send a sample request with a JSON schema. Also we’ll send a minimal “system prompt” template you can tweak.

[14:50] Elena Garcia: Can you include examples for tone? Like empathetic but not overly apologetic.

[14:55] Simran Kaur: Yep.

[15:00] (Fireflies note: transcript skips ahead due to silence / screen share)

[18:42] Priyom Das: …so Markus is showing the console view. You’ll see cost per route, latency, errors. The key thing is the breakdown is per model version.

[18:53] Jamie Chen: That’s nice. We’ve had tools that just give one blended number.

[19:01] Rohan Mehta: Does it show time-to-first-token?

[19:03] Markus Klein: Yeah, TTFT and total. For streaming it matters.

[19:12] Rohan Mehta: Good.

[19:15] Dinesh Patel: And audit logs? Do we get a record of key usage?

[19:18] Markus Klein: Yes. Audit logs include key creation, rotation, and access events. For the demo tenant we can show a sanitized version.

[19:28] Priyom Das: For the POC we won’t over-index on audit logs, but for security review we can provide the FAQ and SOC2 letter under NDA.

[19:38] Dinesh Patel: Okay.

[20:01] Simran Kaur: One more technical note: for your schema, we should keep it simple. The more nested the JSON, the more likely it is to break. Arrays of strings, enums, etc.

[20:12] Rohan Mehta: Agree.

[20:16] Jamie Chen: Also we want citations sometimes. Like quote the ticket line.

[20:21] Simran Kaur: We can do “evidence_snippets” as an array, and instruct it to copy exact spans from the ticket.

[20:30] Rohan Mehta: That helps hallucination.

[20:34] Priyom Das: Awesome. On the commercial side, if the POC passes, likely next step is either hosted usage with higher limits or Dedicated capacity depending on predictable throughput needs.

[20:46] Jamie Chen: If this becomes agent-assist, we’ll need predictable. We’ve had noisy-neighbor issues.

[20:52] Priyom Das: That’s where Dedicated is a fit. But let’s earn it with the POC.

[21:01] (cross talk)

[21:02] Elena Garcia: What about data residency? Not for us, but leadership might ask.

[21:06] Markus Klein: We can speak to it. For Private/VPC we can deploy into your VPC, customer-managed networking, KMS integration. For POC we’re hosted US.

[21:18] Elena Garcia: Got it.

[21:25] (Fireflies note: transcript jumps)

[28:10] Rohan Mehta: …and for throughput, if we run 50 concurrent drafts, are we going to hit a limit?

[28:17] Simran Kaur: We’ll size the demo/POC quota and the underlying capacity for expected concurrency. For the demo tenant, we can reserve enough GPU pool for your window. If we see contention, we’ll schedule your load test time.

[28:32] Rohan Mehta: That’s fair. We can run the big load test at night.

[28:36] Jamie Chen: As long as the interactive tests during business hours are stable.

[28:41] Markus Klein: Yep.

[29:03] Priyom Das: Any other stakeholders we should include? Like procurement or legal?

[29:07] Jamie Chen: Not until we have results.

[29:09] Dinesh Patel: Security will want a short architecture overview. But after.

[29:13] Priyom Das: Okay.

[30:02] Priyom Das: Let’s recap next steps. Markus will provision the project and key tomorrow. Jamie and Rohan will send synthetic tickets by Friday. Simran will share a recommended schema and prompt template, plus a throughput plan. Then we schedule the technical session next week.

[30:19] Jamie Chen: Works.

[30:20] Rohan Mehta: Yep.

[30:22] Dinesh Patel: Works.

[30:24] Elena Garcia: Good.

[31:00] Priyom Das: Cool. Anything else before we drop?

[31:04] Jamie Chen: Just one. Can we get a single page that says “what we will show in the executive review”? Like the demo flow.

[31:11] Priyom Das: Yes. We’ll include that in the POC plan.

[31:16] Markus Klein: And we’ll have a backup mode—screenshots and canned outputs—so you’re not blocked by, like, internet gremlins.

[31:24] Jamie Chen: Thank you.

[31:26] Priyom Das: Great. We’ll follow up in email today.

[31:31] Meeting ended (early). (Fireflies: remaining time accounted for by post-call notes / recording buffer.)
